passages.happening:
God tells Ezekiel to prophesy against the prophets of Israel ‘who prophesy out of their own imagination’ (verse 2). ‘Woe to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit, yet have seen nothing’ (verse 3). They are ‘like foxes among the ruins’ (verse 4). They did not go up into the gaps or repair the wall before the day of battle (verse 5). They claim to speak for the LORD ‘when the LORD did not send them’ (verse 6).

They have led God's people astray, promising peace ‘when there is no peace’ and ‘whitewashing any flimsy wall that is built’ (verse 10). So God will send torrents of rain, hailstones and a windstorm, and the wall will fall, with its foundation laid bare (verses 11-14). Then people will ask where the whitewash is (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Walls were built of stone or mud brick and coated with lime or clay plaster. A thin coat of whitewash could make a poorly built wall look sound, but a heavy storm would wash it off and bring the weak wall down. A true prophet's task was to stand in the gaps and repair the wall: to call the people to turn and to pray for them. These prophets plastered over the cracks with reassuring words. Foxes among ruins are scavengers making their dens in the rubble.

Jeremiah faced the same prophets in Jerusalem. One of them, Hananiah, promised in 594 or 593 BC that the exiles would be home within two years. Jeremiah also named two false prophets among the exiles in Babylon.
passages.later: The law's test was plain: if a prophet's word ‘does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken’ (Deuteronomy 18:22). Hananiah promised a return ‘Within two years’ (Jeremiah 28:3).
passages.hard:
How can anyone tell a true prophet from a false one, if both claim to speak for God?

Ezekiel's hearers faced exactly this, and the Old Testament gives several tests. Deuteronomy 18 says a prophet whose word does not come to pass has not spoken from God. Deuteronomy 13 says that even a prophet whose sign comes true must be rejected if he leads people after other gods. Ezekiel adds a moral test: false prophets discourage the righteous and comfort the wicked (verse 22), and they tell people what they want to hear. None of these tests is instant; the exiles had to wait and see. But the pattern is clear. A true word calls people to God and to turning from wrong, even when it is unwelcome.
passages.asks: The false prophets painted over cracks instead of repairing them. Ask where you prefer comfortable words to true ones. And ask whom you trust to tell you the truth when it is hard to hear.

passages.t: Charms, veils and souls set free
passages.happening:
God turns to ‘the daughters of your people who prophesy out of their own imagination’ (verse 17). ‘Woe to the women who sew magic charms on their wrists and make veils for the heads of people of every height, in order to ensnare their souls’ (verse 18). They have profaned God ‘for handfuls of barley and scraps of bread’ (verse 19), bringing death to those who should live and life to those who should die.

God will tear off their charms and veils, ‘So I will free the souls you have ensnared like birds’ (verse 20). They have disheartened the righteous and encouraged the wicked, and God will deliver his people from their hands (verses 22-23).
passages.hearers:
These women seem to have practiced a form of divination or magic. What the objects were is uncertain. The charms and veils were probably amulets and coverings used in rituals to bind or control, a practice known from Mesopotamian magic, where knotting and binding were common. They were paid in barley and bread, which suggests they served ordinary people for small fees.

The charge is not that they were women. Israel had true women prophets, Miriam, Deborah and Huldah among them. The charge is that they used false words and magic to manipulate life and death.
passages.later: Jeremiah warned, ‘They are filling you with false hopes. They speak visions from their own minds’ (Jeremiah 23:16). Huldah was a true prophet whom King Josiah's officials consulted (2 Kings 22:14).
passages.asks: God set free people who had been trapped by false words. Ask whether anything has a hold on you through fear or superstition. And ask what freedom God offers instead.
